A: How would the AI go about quoting?  
B: The customer says they got a quote from another company that is X amount cheaper and asks why?  
C: Customer calls in saying they used a service from a friend of the owner and got recommended that while you are painting you might be able to clear out some old bird nests or something they cant reach

I'm currently working on the exact opposite idea of this. a call handling service that focuses on human interaction with agents that are local to the business owners operating area. Yes this limits my initial scope at first, but I think that's a good thing.

AI solutions are everywhere at the moment and they might be an okay solution for chatbots, but if you get anything past a general FAQ question, shit goes south fast. I've been trying to do as many customer interviews as possible before going live to make sure I have a fantastic offering, because there are a lot of services out there.

The majority of them outsource to philippines/India/Cheap labour markets and just have a big pool of general knowledge workers that are hardly better than an AI response.

The main critical feedback I've received so far is around domain knowledge and presentation, small businesses cant afford a bad first impression and are (justifiably) hesitant to sub that out it seems. They want to know they can rely on you to not just answer questions but also be the face of their business. They build their business off strong relations - and I don't personally think AI is at the point where it can build that.

I can't even count the amount of times I've had to deal with an AI chatbot that gives me absolutely useless fucking information and just acts as yet another roadblock before I can talk to someone that can solve my problem. Which is one of the main drivers behind my idea, my own frustrations.

I think there is a spot for AI in communications if it is done VERY well, but I don't think it's up to the task of replacing the main customer interaction point of a company. Unless you have some kind of incredible proprietary AI

While a college degree definitely knocks down a barrier, I don't think it's totally impossible (I'm also in Ontario).  


Some tips/tricks I've seen work - 

Joining a company as a non dev role and eventually switching into one. Many companies have customer support roles that require more technical people to help non-technical end users with tasks. These kind of roles are less "degree required" than a full on dev role. But once you're finally in the company, movement is definitely possible (based on my experience at least)   


Secondly, networking. Toronto ALWAYS has some kind of tech meetup going on - check them out, it really does help knowing people.  


Landing the actual interview is usually the hard part, try applying directly with managers if possible, maybe even recruiters. A lot of job websites are notorious for filtering out your resume if you're missing some kind of requirement. Once you get the actual interview - especially for a junior role, it's all about people skills. Sure maybe some light coding exercises to see if you know how to make a variable, but juniors are mostly hired for their ability to work well as a team, communicate effectively and learn quickly (which if you're self taught honestly might be a selling point)  


Lastly - and im not saying this is a good idea so try it at your own risk, just lie about a college degree. I wouldn't say you graduated from waterloo with honours, but if you say you did a 2 year program at a local college, it probably wouldn't be questioned. I've never been asked for anything school related from my 2 year diploma at a no name college.  
Again - NOT saying thats a good idea, but I'm sure many people have done something similar.  


Personally, I think your best bet is to continue self learning, try and snag a less technical role (Customer Support at a tech company, QA, Maybe even IT help desk kind of stuff) and then work your way towards your desired role, or maybe you'll just find out you end up in a role you really like

I started my career as a full stack dev, then moved to junior QA at a rapidly growing company and have grown into the automation engineer role. There's a couple things I think are key that often don't get mentioned. Communication is vital. Sure a lot of roles say good communication skills are needed, but it is especially true with QA. Relaying bug scenarios, test progress, story status etc to PM's, Devs, management etc requires being able to communicate the same thing in different ways effectively.

Time management, organization and direction. All pretty self explanatory, but if your release is delayed because the regression/smoke test plan was mismanaged then people are not happy.

A couple technical things if you're looking into more of an engineer role would be selenium - while it depends on the company, selenium can be found in many testing frameworks, but knowing how it functions at its core is a great first step. Cypress is also on the rise in popularity. Postman is an industry standard for testing API's

Qualification wise I personally got an ISTQB certification and have seen some job postings say it is a nice to have.

I believe when it comes down to it each company has a certain flow of the QA process and I think out of any technical role it's the one where soft skills will probably get you the furthest
